{"id":"PKIX-rgc6","title":"SMTP-DANE (RFC 7672): dedicated entry point, not a reuse of the HTTPS DANE path","description":"## Why

RFC 7672 SMTP-DANE has the strongest production deployment of any DANE flavour — MTAs negotiating TLS routinely use it for trust. A workspace that adopts DANE for HTTPS and not SMTP is incomplete. Replaces PKIX-j32w.6, which asked the question against a function (verify_smtp_signer) that does not exist and would have been the wrong home anyway: SMTP-DANE validates a mail SERVER's TLS certificate, not a signer.

## Why this cannot reuse verify_tls_server's DANE path

Three behavioural differences from HTTPS-DANE. The first makes a shared path wrong rather than merely incomplete.

### 1. Usage filtering — CONFIRM THIS FIRST

Current understanding is that RFC 7672 requires SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) records outright, because public CA trust is not meaningful between MTAs with no user to see a warning: only DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) apply.

THIS IS NOT CONFIRMED. Read RFC 7672 §3.1 and the surrounding text before writing any code. If it holds, then a shared code path with verify_tls_server would honour usage-0 and usage-1 records that SMTP-DANE requires be ignored — a silent policy violation, and the reason this needs its own entry point. If it does not hold, re-evaluate whether a shared path with a mode flag is adequate after all.

### 2. DNSSEC-validated MX lookup — reaches into the resolver

The TLSA owner name derives from an MX lookup, and that lookup must itself be DNSSEC-validated. An unvalidated MX lookup lets an attacker rewrite the MX record and point the connection at a server whose TLSA record they also control, which defeats the whole mechanism.

This is a pkix-dane-resolver requirement, not a wrapper concern: it needs a validated multi-step lookup (MX, then TLSA under the resulting hostname), with the DNSSEC status of BOTH steps surfaced. pkix-dane's TlsaResolver trait as shipped resolves a single TlsaName and has no MX concept. Expect either an additional trait method or a sibling trait in pkix-dane-resolver. Check whether this changes what PKIX-j32w.2 should build before that bead starts.

### 3. Reference identity

Which name the certificate must match follows RFC 7672's MX-derived rules rather than RFC 6125 hostname matching. Determine how this composes with pkix-identity rather than reimplementing name matching.

## Placement — open

PKIX-j32w.6 left this open: pkix-chain wrapper, or a sibling pkix-smtp crate. Decide once the resolver-side shape from difference 2 is known, since an MX-aware resolver trait may make a sibling crate the natural home.

## Also in scope

- RFC 7672's own opportunistic-vs-mandatory posture at the SMTP level, and how it composes with the DaneFailurePolicy decided in PKIX-j32w.4. These are different layers and may not agree; work out which wins.
- Whether the dane / dane-resolver feature split decided on PKIX-j32w.3 extends here unchanged.

## Depends on

pkix-dane 0.2.0 (shipped). Resolver work is PKIX-j32w.2; this bead should be read before that one starts, because difference 2 may widen its scope.

## Acceptance

[ ] RFC 7672 usage-filtering requirement confirmed against the RFC text and recorded
[ ] MX lookup is DNSSEC-validated, with the status of both lookup steps surfaced to the caller
[ ] Usage 0 and 1 records handled per the confirmed RFC requirement
[ ] Reference identity follows RFC 7672, composed with pkix-identity rather than reimplemented
[ ] Placement decided and recorded","status":"open","priority":3,"issue_type":"feature","owner":"mark@reviewcommit.com","created_at":"2026-11-24T19:25:04.79877682Z","created_by":"Mark Atwood","updated_at":"2026-11-24T19:25:04.79877682Z"}

{"notes":"RESEARCH DONE 2026-11-24, against the RFC text. THIS BEAD'S CENTRAL PREMISE WAS WRONG and is corrected below. No code written: the bead said to confirm first, and confirming changed the design.

## CORRECTION: usage 0/1 is NOT a MUST-ignore

This bead stated, flagged as unconfirmed, that "RFC 7672 requires SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) records outright" and that a shared code path with verify_tls_server would therefore be "a silent policy violation". That is not what the RFC says.

RFC 7672 section 3.1.3, verbatim:

  "Therefore, TLSA records for the port 25 SMTP service used by client MTAs
   SHOULD NOT include TLSA RRs with certificate usage PKIX-TA(0) or
   PKIX-EE(1)."

  "SMTP client treatment of TLSA RRs with certificate usages PKIX-TA(0) or
   PKIX-EE(1) is undefined.  As with any other unsupported certificate
   usage, SMTP clients MAY treat such records as 'unusable'."

So: SHOULD NOT PUBLISH on the server side, and UNDEFINED with a MAY on the client side. Honouring usage 0/1 in an SMTP client would be implementing undefined behaviour, which is permitted. It is still the wrong thing to do -- the RFC's reasoning is that PKIX usages cannot aid SMTP TLS security because an attacker who can compromise DNSSEC can simply substitute a non-PKIX usage, and MTAs have no agreed CA list and no user to click OK -- but we would be following a MAY, not complying with a MUST. The implementation should say so rather than claiming compliance it does not have.

Consequence: usage filtering NO LONGER CARRIES the separate-entry-point argument. That argument now rests entirely on the two other differences, both of which survive.

## What the RFC actually requires, confirmed

1. DANE-EE(3) name checks, section 3.2.1: "The SMTP client MUST NOT perform certificate name checks". pkix-dane's verify_dane_ee ALREADY does no name check, per RFC 7671 section 5.1. Nothing to do.

2. DANE-TA(2) name checks, section 3.2.2: the client MUST perform name checks, and MUST use the TLSA BASE DOMAIN as the primary reference identifier. Additionally:
   - if the base domain came from a "secure" MX lookup, the original next-hop domain MUST be a second reference identifier
   - the CNAME-expanded original next-hop domain MUST be a third, if different
   - when using DANE despite "insecure" MX redirection, the MX hostname is the ONLY reference identifier
   So this is a SET of reference identifiers derived from the lookup chain, not one hostname. That shape is genuinely different from verify_tls_server's single ServerName.

3. Reference identifier matching, section 3.2.3: only DNS-IDs are matched if any are present; THE CN-ID IS CONSIDERED WHEN NO DNS-IDs ARE PRESENT. Wildcards valid in either, must be the entire first label, and MUST match exactly one label by default.

4. Section 3.2: "When at least one usable 'secure' TLSA record is found, the SMTP client MUST use TLSA records to authenticate the SMTP server. Messages MUST NOT be delivered via the SMTP server if authentication fails." So RFC 7672 is opportunistic about WHETHER DANE is available and MANDATORY once a usable secure record exists. That is a sharper posture than DaneFailurePolicy::Opportunistic and needs reconciling with it, not merely composing.

## NEW BLOCKER FOUND: pkix-identity cannot be reused as-is

RFC 7672 section 3.2.3 requires CN-ID fallback when no DNS-IDs are present. pkix-identity deliberately refuses it. Its rustdoc:

  "Does not consult the certificate's Subject DN CN attribute -- CN fallback
   was deprecated by RFC 6125 section 6.4.4 and is intentionally not
   performed. A certificate that carries identity only in its CN is rejected
   with IdentityError::MissingSan."

Both positions are correct for their context: RFC 6125 deprecated CN fallback for web PKI, and RFC 7672 kept it for MTA-to-MTA where certificates are often ancient and self-managed. But it means SMTP-DANE name checks cannot simply call pkix_identity::verify_dns_name.

Decide before implementing: an opt-in CN-ID mode on pkix-identity, or an SMTP-specific matcher. Leaning toward an opt-in on pkix-identity, since the wildcard and case-folding logic is there and worth reusing, and a second matcher invites the two to diverge -- but it means putting a deprecated-for-web behaviour behind a flag in a crate that currently refuses it on principle, which deserves a deliberate decision.

## Revised scope

Three pieces, in dependency order:

A. Reference-identifier matching for SMTP: the identifier SET from section 3.2.2 plus the matching rules from section 3.2.3, including the CN-ID question above. Pure, testable, no I/O. Smallest piece and the one that unblocks the rest.

B. DNSSEC-validated MX lookup in pkix-dane-resolver: a validated two-step lookup (MX, then TLSA under the resulting hostname) with the DNSSEC status of BOTH steps surfaced, since section 3.2.2's identifier set depends on whether the MX lookup was secure. pkix-dane's TlsaResolver resolves a single TlsaName and has no MX concept. Also needs sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 (MX resolution, non-MX destinations) and 2.1.1 (bogus/indeterminate handling), none of which I have read yet.

C. The entry point itself, and its placement. Still open between a pkix-chain wrapper and a sibling crate; B's shape should decide it.

## Not yet read

Sections 2.1.1 to 2.1.3 (DNS errors, bogus and indeterminate responses, stub resolver considerations), 2.2.1 to 2.2.3 (MX resolution, non-MX destinations, TLSA record lookup), and section 8.1 (SNI support). Piece B should not be designed without them; section 2.1.1 in particular will bear on how DaneFailurePolicy composes.

## Acceptance, revised

[x] RFC 7672 usage-filtering requirement confirmed against the RFC text and recorded -- it is undefined/MAY, not MUST, and this bead's original claim was wrong
[ ] Decide CN-ID: opt-in on pkix-identity, or an SMTP-specific matcher
[ ] Reconcile section 3.2's MUST-authenticate-once-available with DaneFailurePolicy
[ ] Read sections 2.1 and 2.2 before designing the MX lookup
[ ] MX lookup DNSSEC-validated, with the status of both steps surfaced
[ ] Reference identifier set per section 3.2.2, matching per section 3.2.3
[ ] Placement decided and recorded"}

{"notes":"PIECE A DONE 2026-11-24 (name checks). Pieces B (MX lookup) and C (entry point) remain, with the research they need recorded below.

## Done: RFC 7672 §3.2 name checks

- pkix_identity::verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback -- §3.2.3 matching. 14 tests.
- pkix_dane::smtp behind a new `smtp` feature -- SmtpIdentities (the §3.2.2 set), SmtpNameCheck, SmtpNameError, verify_smtp_name. 18 tests.
- Five new pkix-identity fixtures for the CN-ID rule.
- Builds for thumbv7em-none-eabi with the smtp feature; 1990 workspace tests pass.

## Decisions made, with reasons

CN-ID: AN OPT-IN FUNCTION ON pkix-identity, not an SMTP-specific matcher.
RFC 7672 §3.2.3 requires CN fallback; pkix-identity refuses it for the Web PKI per RFC 6125 §6.4.4. Both are right for their protocol. Decided on pkix-identity because there must be exactly ONE wildcard implementation in the workspace -- a second would be a divergence hazard and wildcard bugs are security bugs. It is a separate function rather than a flag so no caller acquires CN fallback by default and the Web PKI path cannot be loosened by passing an argument. It delegates the DNS-ID path to verify_dns_name rather than reimplementing it.

Also note AGENTS.md non-negotiable #5: the workspace commits to standards-body specs. Declining to implement a standards-track IETF requirement anywhere would have been this workspace making policy.

PLACEMENT: a MODULE in pkix-dane behind a feature, not a sibling crate.
Same domain -- SMTP DANE is a profile of DANE -- and it keeps the crate count down while still giving a dedicated entry point, which is what this bead actually asked for. Splitting a module out later is easier than merging crates. The feature gate matters for a second reason: it keeps RFC 7672's CN-ID fallback out of an HTTPS-only consumer's dependency graph.

USAGE 0/1: treated as unusable, documented as TAKING THE MAY in §3.1.3 rather than as compliance. SmtpNameError::PkixUsageUnusable says so in its rustdoc.

## §3.2's MUST and DaneFailurePolicy -- still open, and sharper than filed

§3.2: "When at least one usable 'secure' TLSA record is found, the SMTP client MUST use TLSA records to authenticate the SMTP server. Messages MUST NOT be delivered via the SMTP server if authentication fails."

So RFC 7672 is opportunistic about WHETHER DANE is available and MANDATORY once a usable secure record exists. That is sharper than DaneFailurePolicy::Opportunistic, which permits falling back. The SMTP path must not offer a policy that allows delivery after a failed DANE authentication -- that is not a configuration choice, it is a MUST NOT. Needs reconciling in piece C, not merely composing.

## Research for piece B, the MX lookup -- READ THIS BEFORE DESIGNING IT

§2.2.1, MX resolution:
- TLSA records and the base domain are derived SEPARATELY FOR EACH MX hostname.
- MX records MUST be sorted by preference, AND: "an MX hostname with a worse (numerically higher) MX preference that has TLSA records MUST NOT preempt an MX hostname with a better (numerically lower) preference that has no TLSA records... prevention of delivery loops by obeying MX preferences MUST take precedence over channel security considerations." A naive "prefer the secure MX" implementation VIOLATES a MUST. This is the most surprising requirement in the document.
- CNAME expansion of the initial name, repeated to the MTA's recursion limit.
- Insecure MX RRset (or any CNAME leading to it) + DANE mandatory -> delivery MUST be delayed. Insecure + not mandatory -> free to use pre-DANE opportunistic TLS or cleartext.
- A client MAY still elect DANE TLS with an insecure MX RRset (the hosting-provider case: unsigned customer zone, signed provider zone with TLSA records). That is the case SmtpIdentities::insecure_mx exists for.
- SHOULD log unexpanded MX hostnames from insecure lookups, and "Any successful authentication via an insecurely determined MX host MUST NOT be misrepresented in the mail logs as secure delivery to the intended next-hop domain."
- No TLSA records, or only insecure ones -> DANE not applicable, proceed as pre-DANE opportunistic.
- "any errors during TLSA lookups MUST... cause the SMTP server in question to be treated as unreachable" -- downgrade protection.

§2.2.2, non-MX destinations -- AN ORDERING MUST THAT IS EASY TO MISS:
- "the SMTP client MUST perform any A and/or AAAA queries for the destination BEFORE attempting to locate the associated TLSA records."
- Why: load-balancing nameservers at some large providers mishandle TLSA queries, answering SERVFAIL or NOTIMP instead of an insecure negative reply, which would cause messages to be consistently delayed and ultimately returned to the sender.
- No address records -> unreachable. Address records found but the DNSSEC status of the FIRST query response is insecure -> SHOULD NOT look for TLSA records at all.

§2.1.1, security statuses:
- "indeterminate" is used exclusively in the RFC 4035 sense and "DNS records that would be classified 'indeterminate'... are simply classified as 'insecure'". "All 'insecure' RRsets MUST be handled identically."
- Consequence for us: pkix-dane's DnssecStatus has Secure/Insecure/Indeterminate/Bogus mapping hickory's Proof 1:1. The SMTP path MUST collapse Indeterminate into Insecure. That is a mapping in the SMTP code, not a change to the enum.

## Design note for piece B

The lookup POLICY is pure: which MX to try next, whether this RRset is secure enough, whether to issue a TLSA query at all, are all functions of DNS answers rather than of I/O. So piece B can be a sans-IO state machine in no_std pkix-dane -- the pattern already established by pkix_chain::sans_io -- with pkix-dane-resolver driving it and performing the lookups. That keeps AGENTS.md #1 and the Option C async placement, and makes the surprising MX-preference rule testable without a resolver.

## Not yet read

§2.1.2 (DNS error handling) and §2.1.3 (stub resolver considerations) in full, §6 (mandatory DANE, referenced by §2.2.1), and §8.1 (SNI support).

## Acceptance, revised

[x] RFC 7672 usage-filtering requirement confirmed against the RFC text and recorded -- it is undefined/MAY, not MUST
[x] CN-ID decided: opt-in function on pkix-identity
[x] Reference identifier set per §3.2.2, matching per §3.2.3
[x] Placement decided: a feature-gated module in pkix-dane
[x] §2.1 and §2.2 read before designing the MX lookup
[ ] Reconcile §3.2's MUST-authenticate-once-available with DaneFailurePolicy
[ ] MX lookup DNSSEC-validated, with the status of both steps surfaced, honouring the MX-preference MUST and the A/AAAA-before-TLSA MUST
[ ] The entry point that drives it"}

Three behavioural differences from HTTPS-DANE. The first makes a shared path wrong rather than merely incomplete.

Current understanding is that RFC 7672 requires SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) records outright, because public CA trust is not meaningful between MTAs with no user to see a warning: only DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) apply.

### 2. DNSSEC-validated MX lookup — reaches into the resolver

The TLSA owner name derives from an MX lookup, and that lookup must itself be DNSSEC-validated. An unvalidated MX lookup lets an attacker rewrite the MX record and point the connection at a server whose TLSA record they also control, which defeats the whole mechanism.

## THE FAILURE-POLICY QUESTION, RESOLVED DIFFERENTLY THAN FILED

This bead expected to reconcile section 3.2's MUST NOT with DaneFailurePolicy, probably by offering an SMTP function that takes no policy so it CANNOT fall back.

Mark redirected it: messages should still be deliverable when DANE fails, we just need to know it failed so they can be tagged, routed, or processed.

That is the better design and it dissolves the problem rather than solving it. The function REPORTS; it does not decide. Every outcome is Ok, including authentication failure, and there is no policy parameter at all -- not because fallback is forbidden, but because the verdict is an input to the MTA's decision rather than a substitute for it. An MTA cannot tag or route on a DANE failure that arrives indistinguishable from a malformed call.

So:
- SmtpDaneVerdict::{Authenticated, NotApplicable, Failed}, all Ok
- rfc7672_permits_delivery() is section 3.2's MUST NOT as a predicate, false only for Failed -- a conforming MTA is one line away, a non-conforming one has to visibly ignore it
- is_authenticated() is the narrower question, because a log claiming a secure channel needs that one and not the first
- SmtpDaneFailure separates four operational problems, since an MTA reporting to a postmaster wants to say which

The rustdoc states the REASON behind the MUST NOT rather than just citing it: a failure where usable secure records exist means either the server is misconfigured or the connection is intercepted, and the sender cannot tell which. It also records that delivering-with-the-failure-logged is coherent for deployments the RFC was not written for, such as a staged rollout measuring DANE before enforcing it in the manner of DMARC p=none.

Keeping NotApplicable and Failed apart is the point of the type. Collapsing them would let a log claim an authenticated channel for a cleartext delivery, or read active interception as a quiet absence of DANE.

## Section 6 was incomplete and is now fixed

Reading section 6 before the entry point, as this bead required, found a real gap: "With mandatory DANE TLS, when no usable TLSA records are found, message delivery is delayed." `mandatory` was being enforced only at the MX step, so a server that published nothing usable was still offered for UNAUTHENTICATED delivery -- defeating the policy it was set for.

Fixed: a host without usable records is passed over, the next in preference order is tried, and delivery is delayed only when none has any. New DelayReason::MandatoryDaneWithoutUsableTlsa, distinct from MandatoryDaneWithInsecureMx because the remedies differ -- the first is the receiving domain's TLSA records, the second its DNSSEC.

First attempt at this was wrong in two ways worth remembering: it delayed on the FIRST host without records rather than trying the next, and the "skipped for want of TLSA" flag survived a later host succeeding. Both caught by tests.

## No trust-store parameter, which was a late simplification

DANE-EE(3) validates no path. DANE-TA(2) validates to the anchor its own record supplies and to that anchor ALONE -- merging it with a caller's store would implement "DANE-TA or any CA", weaker than either, and pkix-chain's existing dane.rs already had that right with a comment saying so. PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1), the two usages that would consult a store, are unusable here per section 3.1.3.

So no code path reads caller anchors, and the signature stopped accepting them. The first draft merged the DANE anchor into the caller's anchors, which would have been the exact weakening dane.rs warns about.

This bead claimed RFC 7672 REQUIRES SMTP clients to ignore PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1), making a shared code path with the HTTPS entry point a policy violation. Section 3.1.3 says servers SHOULD NOT publish them for port 25 and leaves client treatment UNDEFINED, with a MAY to treat them as unusable. Honouring them would have been permitted.

The separate entry point was still right, but on the other two differences -- the identifier set and the DNSSEC-validated MX lookup. The implementation documents that it TAKES the MAY rather than claiming conformance it does not have.

## The failure-policy question was resolved differently than filed

The plan was an SMTP function taking no failure policy so it COULD NOT fall back after a DANE failure. Mark redirected: messages should stay deliverable, we just need to know DANE failed so they can be tagged, routed or processed.

That is better and it dissolves the problem. The function REPORTS; it does not decide. All three outcomes are Ok, including failure, and there is no policy parameter -- not because fallback is forbidden but because the verdict is an input to the MTA's decision. An MTA cannot tag or route on a failure indistinguishable from a malformed call.

rfc7672_permits_delivery() carries section 3.2's MUST NOT as a predicate, so a conforming MTA is one line away and a non-conforming one visibly ignores it. is_authenticated() is the narrower question, because NotApplicable also permits delivery and a log claiming a secure channel needs the second.

## Decisions, with reasons

CN-ID went to pkix-identity as a separately-named opt-in function, not an SMTP-specific matcher, so the workspace keeps exactly ONE wildcard implementation -- a second would be a divergence hazard and wildcard bugs are security bugs. Also AGENTS.md #5: declining to implement a standards-track IETF requirement anywhere would have been this workspace making policy.

Sans-IO for discovery, which cost less than expected. The decisions are pure functions of DNS answers, so the two surprising MUSTs are testable by scripting answers rather than standing up a resolver, and the async driver became a thin loop that cannot get the ordering wrong because it only answers what it is asked.

No trust-store parameter on the entry point. DANE-EE validates no path; DANE-TA validates to its own record's anchor ALONE, since merging would implement "DANE-TA or any CA"; and the two usages that would consult a store are unusable here. The first draft merged them, which pkix-chain's existing dane.rs already warns against in a comment.

## The two MUSTs a naive implementation violates

MX PREFERENCE OUTRANKS CHANNEL SECURITY (2.2.1). A worse-preference host with TLSA records must not preempt a better-preference host without them. Preferring the DANE-capable host is a conformance bug and the obvious thing to write. Mutation-tested: reversing the sort fails that test and two others.

ADDRESS LOOKUPS PRECEDE TLSA LOOKUPS (2.2.2), and with an insecure address answer no TLSA query is issued AT ALL. That is the half that protects against load-balancing nameservers at large providers which answer TLSA with SERVFAIL instead of an insecure negative reply -- a query never sent cannot strand a message.

## Gaps found by reading rather than by guessing

Reading section 6 before the entry point, as this bead required, found that `mandatory` was enforced only at the MX step -- so a server publishing nothing usable was still offered for UNAUTHENTICATED delivery, defeating the policy it was set for. Now the host is passed over, the next tried, and delivery delayed only when none has usable records.

Reading section 2.1.1 found that "indeterminate" folds into "insecure" for this profile. Collapsed at the boundary in RrsetTrust so no decision site has to remember.

Section 2.2.1's "the MX RRset (or any CNAME leading to it)" means an insecure CNAME taints an otherwise-signed MX RRset. A last-answer-wins implementation misses it; the machine only ever weakens mx_secure.

## Gap found by live testing, which a synthetic fixture would not have caught

huque.com publishes PKIX-EE(1) ALONGSIDE DANE-EE(3). TlsaRecord::is_usable asks whether a record parses and carries an assigned usage, not whether this profile can authenticate with it -- so usage-0 and usage-1 records survived discovery's filter and made dane_records() report Some, claiming DANE applied when nothing present could authenticate, and under mandatory policy offering such a host instead of delaying.

Fixed: dane_records() and identities() require a DANE-EE or DANE-TA record. The records are still CARRIED in tlsa_response(), deliberately, because the entry point needs them to report "published only PKIX usages" distinctly from "published nothing" -- a misconfiguration worth telling a postmaster about.

Worth noting as a method: the live test found this by failing on a wrong assumption about a real zone. A synthetic PKIX-only fixture would have tested the filter and missed the mixed case entirely.

BasicTlsProfile sets require_subject_alt_name, correct for the Web PKI and wrong here, so it rejects the CN-only certificates section 3.2.3 exists to accommodate -- during PATH VALIDATION, reporting PathValidationFailed(MissingSan), which points nowhere near the profile. Documented on the function, but documentation does not help someone who reaches for the obvious profile.
